claims.text: Multiphase refractory or eutectic high-entropy alloys are the material family of interest.
Tensile ductility is the primary mechanical property of interest.
These alloys will undergo a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during thermal aging.
The initial ductile state is governed by a disordered or semi-coherent matrix that permits easy dislocation glide.
Aging induces chemical ordering and phase evolution in these multiphase alloys.
An intermediate brittle, highly ordered phase with high lattice mismatch or incoherent interfaces impedes dislocations, creates stress concentrations, and sharply reduces ductility.
The relevant intermediate ordered phase may have an L12, D0a, or B2 structure.
Heusler or sigma intermetallic phases formed during aging may act as brittle structural mediators.
The volume fraction, size, and interfacial coherency of ordered precipitates govern the aging-dependent mechanical response.
Coherent precipitation structures can preserve a combination of high strength and tensile ductility.
Incoherent or brittle ordered phases cause brittleness.
Continued aging can coarsen ordered precipitates, lower their obstacle number density, and relax interfacial stresses.
Precipitate coarsening or transformation to a less brittle ordered phase restores ductility by enabling Orowan bypass or precipitate shearing.
Tensile elongation will begin above 15%, fall below 5% at approximately 100–200 hours, and recover to 10–15% after more than 500 hours of aging.
Ultimate tensile strength will peak at the intermediate brittle stage because order hardening is maximal there.
The transition requires an aging temperature high enough to produce substantial chemical ordering but below the temperature at which the ordered phase becomes unstable or coarsens immediately.
The transition requires formation of a distinct brittle ordered phase that is absent from the initial state.
Ductility recovery may not occur when the brittle phase remains thermodynamically stable and neither coarsens sufficiently nor transforms.
